explanations.explanation: Yes, his nurse. Jehosheba, King Joram's daughter and Ahaziah's sister, tucks little Joash and the nurse into a bedroom. The text says she did it to hide him from Athaliah, Ahaziah's mother. Little guy didn't get a vote, but he got a caretaker, and that's a good deal.

The text doesn't put his mother in that bedroom. It says Jehosheba hid Joash, Ahaziah's little son, along with his nurse. So the one by his side is a nurse. Don't go looking for a mother in that room, because the verse never brings her up.

No uncle in this verse, friend. Jehosheba, Ahaziah's sister, puts Joash and his nurse in a bedroom to hide him from Athaliah. Jehosheba is the one doing the rescuing, and the nurse is the one sticking with him. That's the whole hiding crew.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it. Joash stays hidden with his nurse in the house of the LORD while Athaliah rules the land. Think about that for a second. The one place nobody thinks to look is the place that's right in front of everybody.

I see why a hiding story sends your mind to a cave. David hid in the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1). But in this passage, Joash and his nurse stay hidden in the house of the LORD. Different hideout, different story.

Not a palace for this little one. The text says Joash remained hidden with his nurse in the house of the LORD. A palace is the kind of place you'd get found in a hurry. The house of the LORD is where he stays for six years.

True. The text says Joash remained hidden for six years while Athaliah ruled the land. So there's a ruler on the throne, and a little king-to-be tucked away where she can't reach him. Hold onto that picture, because the next part flips it.

Close, but the verse says it plainly: Joash stayed hidden for six years while Athaliah ruled the land. She isn't gone or sitting out. She's the one in charge during all that hiding. That's what makes the hiding matter.

Yes! Jehoiada the priest shows the commanders the king's son, and that's Joash, Ahaziah's little boy. After six years of keeping him tucked away, the secret finally comes out into the open. I bet those commanders had a lot to think about in that moment.

Elisha isn't in this scene. The text says Jehoiada the priest shows the commanders the king's son, who is Joash. This is a priest and soldiers meeting inside the house of the LORD. The prophet isn't on the guest list.

Jehu isn't in this room, friend. After the covenant and the oath, Jehoiada the priest shows the commanders the king's son. That's Joash, Ahaziah's little boy, the one who's been hidden away. This is all happening in Judah, with Judah's own royal family.

explanations.answer: They must be put to death
explanations.explanation: That's right. Jehoiada says, “…anyone who approaches the ranks must be put to death.” (2 Kings 11:8) He is not playing around. The king is surrounded, weapons in hand, and the ranks are off limits.

No questions at the door here. The order is that anyone who approaches the ranks must be put to death. Jehoiada has the guards surround the king with weapons in hand. There's no interview process for the people who come near.

explanations.answer: They must be sent back home
explanations.explanation: No polite escort home. Jehoiada's order in verse 8 is that anyone who approaches the ranks must be put to death. That's how seriously he wants the king protected. The guards are surrounding him with weapons in hand.

True. Jehoiada says, “You must stay close to the king wherever he goes.” (2 Kings 11:8) So that's an order to guard him with weapons in hand and not wander off. Where Joash goes, the guards go. Talk about a bodyguard who never takes a break.

The text says the opposite. Jehoiada tells the guards, “You must stay close to the king wherever he goes.” (2 Kings 11:8) So the guards are told to stay close, with weapons in hand. No drifting off to grab a snack. That would be a cookie break, and nobody gets one.

David it is. Jehoiada gives the commanders the spears and shields of King David from the house of the LORD. Those weapons are kept in the house of the LORD, and now they're handed out for this moment. That's some serious gear to get from the back room.

Saul's name isn't on these spears and shields. The text says Jehoiada gives the commanders the spears and shields of King David from the house of the LORD. So the weapons come with David's name on them. Saul isn't mentioned in this passage.

Solomon is a good guess, since he was David's son. He took his seat on his father David's throne (1 Kings 2:12). But the text says Jehoiada hands over the spears and shields of King David. So these come straight from David, not Solomon.

The crown, yes. Jehoiada brings out the king's son and puts the crown on him. That's Joash, Ahaziah's little boy, the one who's been hidden for six years. That's quite a way to go from the bedroom to a crowned head.
A robe could fit a king, but it's not what the text says. Jehoiada brings out the king's son and puts the crown on him. That's the item named in this verse, and it's on Joash's head.
A ring is a fair thing to picture with a king, but this verse doesn't mention one. Jehoiada brings out the king's son and puts the crown on him. So the answer is a crown. That's what goes on Joash.

Right. After Jehoiada crowns Joash, gives him the Testimony and proclaims him king, they anoint him. The crown, the Testimony, the proclamation and the anointing all pile up in one verse. I think that's a lot to take in for a seven-year-old, but he's got a crowd cheering him on.
No foot washing in this scene. The text says that after the crown, the Testimony and the proclamation, they anoint him. So the next thing on Joash is the anointing. Feet can stay dry.

explanations.answer: They give him a new name
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give Joash a new name here. It says Jehoiada crowns him, presents him with the Testimony and proclaims him king, and then they anoint him. He stays Joash the whole way through. So it's an anointing, not a rename.

Not quite. The text says the people clapped their hands and declared, “Long live the king!” (2 Kings 11:12) That's not silent at all. It's the sound of a crowd cheering for their new king. Silent would be a very quiet coronation.
False is right. The text says the people clapped their hands and declared, “Long live the king!” (2 Kings 11:12) That's clapping and shouting, not silence. After all that hiding, the quiet is over.

The new king, yes. Athaliah looks out and sees the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom. That's Joash, the little one she didn't know was alive. I think that is a very rough surprise for her.

Elisha isn't in this scene. When Athaliah looks out, the text says she sees the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom. That's the new king, Joash. The officers, trumpeters and people are all around him.

Jehu isn't the one standing there. Athaliah sees the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom. That's Joash, the new king of Judah, with officers and trumpeters beside him. Jehu isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage.

Treason it is. Athaliah tears her clothes and screams, “Treason! Treason!” (2 Kings 11:14) She says it twice, and loud. That's what she hollers when she sees the king crowned and the people rejoicing.

She doesn't scream that word. The text says Athaliah tears her clothes and screams, “Treason! Treason!” (2 Kings 11:14) That's the word she picks when she sees the new king. Murder isn't what comes out of her mouth.

Not robbery, friend. When Athaliah sees the new king, the people rejoicing and the trumpets blowing, she tears her clothes and screams, “Treason! Treason!” (2 Kings 11:14) That's the word the text gives. Nothing about stolen goods.

The text says the opposite. Jehoiada's order comes with a reason: “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.” (2 Kings 11:15) So he has her brought out between the ranks first. The house of the LORD is where he doesn't want it done.

False is right. The text says, “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.” (2 Kings 11:15) So Jehoiada orders the commanders to bring her out between the ranks. The place matters to him, and he says so plainly.

explanations.answer: At the horses' entrance to the palace grounds
explanations.explanation: Yes. The commanders seize Athaliah as she reaches the horses' entrance to the palace grounds, and there she is put to death. That's outside the house of the LORD, just as Jehoiada ordered. The text gives the exact spot.

explanations.answer: At the Fish Gate of the city
explanations.explanation: There is a Fish Gate in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:3), but it's not the spot in this passage. The text says they seize Athaliah as she reaches the horses' entrance to the palace grounds. That's where she is put to death. So the Fish Gate isn't part of this story.

explanations.answer: At the Valley Gate of the city
explanations.explanation: The Valley Gate is mentioned in Nehemiah 3:13, but it's not in this scene. The commanders seize Athaliah as she reaches the horses' entrance to the palace grounds. That's the place the text names. It's a different gate from the one you picked.

explanations.answer: That they would be the LORD's people
explanations.explanation: That's the covenant. Jehoiada makes a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people that they would be the LORD's people. That's the heart of it, and it's the biggest promise in the whole scene. It's more than a crown. It's a promise about who they belong to.

explanations.answer: That they would never go to war again
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about war in this covenant. It says Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people that they would be the LORD's people. That's what they promise. Not a peace treaty, but a promise about belonging to the LORD.

explanations.answer: That they would rebuild the city walls
explanations.explanation: No wall building in this covenant. The text says Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people that they would be the LORD's people. That's the whole promise here. Walls aren't mentioned.

True. Jehoiada makes a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people, and he also makes a covenant between the king and the people. That's two covenants, one right after the other. The man was busy that day.

The text says there's a second covenant. After the one between the LORD and the king and the people, Jehoiada also makes a covenant between the king and the people. That's two covenants in the same verse. So this one is true.

Idols, yes. The people of the land go to the temple of Baal, tear it down, and smash the altars and idols to pieces. That's a lot of smashing. I think there was a lot of noise, and not a single thing left standing.
Lampstands aren't what the text names. The people tear down the temple of Baal and smash the altars and idols to pieces. So it's the altars and the idols that get smashed. Lampstands stay out of it.

No scrolls in this verse, friend. The people of the land tear down the temple of Baal, and they smash the altars and idols to pieces. That's the list the text gives. Idols are what go with the altars.

The throne, yes. They enter the royal palace by way of the Gate of the Guards, and then Joash takes his seat on the royal throne. From a hidden bedroom to the royal throne. That's a big move for one little king.

A chariot would be quite the ride, but it's not what the text says. They bring the king down to the royal palace, and then Joash takes his seat on the royal throne. That's the seat the verse names. No chariot in sight.

A balcony is a nice place for a wave, but the text doesn't mention one. Joash enters the royal palace and takes his seat on the royal throne. So it's the throne that gets the king. That's the seat that matters in this verse.
The text says the opposite. After Athaliah is put to the sword, all the people of the land rejoice, and the city is quiet. So there's no uproar in the city. It's peaceful after all that noise.

False is right. The text says all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet because Athaliah had been put to the sword at the royal palace. So after the shouting and the trumpets, the city settles down. Quiet at last.
Seven, yes. The text says, “Joash was seven years old when he became king.” (2 Kings 11:21) That's a tiny king on a big throne. I think his feet didn't reach the floor, but that's just my guess.
Nine is a little too high. The text says, “Joash was seven years old when he became king.” (2 Kings 11:21) So he's even younger than your pick. Seven is the number the verse gives.
Eleven is quite a bit older than he is. The text says, “Joash was seven years old when he became king.” (2 Kings 11:21) That's the age the verse gives, no rounding up. He's a very young king.
